cards.q: What is the difference between a static library and a DLL?
cards.a: A static library's code is copied into the executable at link time. A DLL's code stays in its own file and is mapped into the process when the program loads it, so it can be shared and replaced separately.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: Name three reasons to put code in a DLL.
cards.a: Sharing one copy between programs, updating that part without rebuilding the programs, loading code at run time (plugins), reloading code while running, and offering a C interface to other languages.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: What file format do DLLs and executables share?
cards.a: The PE (Portable Executable) format.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: List the loader's steps for one module.
cards.a: Find the file, map it, relocate it if needed, load its dependencies, bind its imports into the import address table, run its initialisation.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: What is an RVA?
cards.a: A relative virtual address: an offset from the start of a module in memory. The real address is the module's base plus the RVA.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: Why are dependencies initialised first?
cards.a: So that when a DLL's initialisation runs, every DLL it calls into is already ready.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: What does `__declspec(dllexport)` do?
cards.a: It puts the function (or class, or variable) into the DLL's export table so other modules can find it by name.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: Which two files does building a DLL project produce that you need, and when is each needed?
cards.a: The `.dll`, needed at run time next to the program, and the import `.lib`, needed at link time by programs that call it.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: What does the `STONEMATH_EXPORTS` symbol do?
cards.a: It is defined only in the DLL project, so the shared header can choose `dllexport` there and `dllimport` everywhere else.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: What three things does an export table entry hold?
cards.a: A name (optional), an ordinal, and the RVA of the function or variable.

cards.q: Give two reasons to use a .def file.
cards.a: To give fixed ordinals, to export under a different name than the code uses, or to export plain names without changing the code.

cards.q: Why prefer exporting a function over exporting a variable?
cards.a: A function can change how it works internally without breaking callers; a variable fixes its type and meaning for every program that uses it.

cards.q: What is the import address table?
cards.a: An array of slots in a module, one for each imported function, that the loader fills with the real addresses at load time. Calls into DLLs jump through those slots.

cards.q: Why does `__declspec(dllimport)` make calls slightly better?
cards.a: The compiler can call through the IAT slot directly instead of calling a stub that then jumps through the slot.

cards.q: Why should a published DLL never remove an export?
cards.a: Programs built against it import that name, and the loader refuses to start them if it is missing.

cards.q: How do you tell whether a DLL is 32-bit or 64-bit?
cards.a: `dumpbin /headers` shows the machine type: x86 or x64.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: Where can you see which file a running program actually loaded for a DLL?
cards.a: In the debugger's Modules window (the Path column), or in Process Monitor.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: What does the Dependencies tool add over dumpbin?
cards.a: The whole dependency tree recursively, with missing DLLs highlighted, and correct handling of API set names.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: What is a decorated (mangled) name?
cards.a: The symbol name the compiler gives a C++ function, encoding its name, scope, calling convention, return and parameter types, so overloads can coexist.

cards.q: What does `extern "C"` give up?
cards.a: Overloading, and C++-only types in signatures if other languages are to call the function.

cards.q: Decode `?reset@@YAXXZ`.
cards.a: `void __cdecl reset(void)`: a free function `reset` returning `void` (`X`) with no parameters (`XZ`).

cards.q: What does a calling convention decide?
cards.a: Where arguments and the return value go, which registers a function may change, and who cleans the arguments off the stack.

cards.q: Why does the calling convention matter more across a DLL boundary than inside one program?
cards.a: The two sides were compiled separately, so nothing guarantees they agree unless the interface says so.

cards.q: Give the 32-bit decorated names for `int f(int, double)` as `__cdecl` and as `__stdcall`.
cards.a: `_f` and `_f@12` (4 bytes for the int plus 8 for the double).

cards.q: What do LoadLibraryW, GetProcAddress and FreeLibrary each do?
cards.a: Map a DLL and get its handle; look up an exported function's address by name; drop one reference to the DLL and unmap it when none remain.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: What happens to function pointers from a DLL after its last FreeLibrary?
cards.a: They dangle: the code they point to is no longer mapped, so calling them crashes.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: Name two things run-time loading makes possible that load-time linking does not.
cards.a: Starting without the DLL, choosing between DLLs, plugins found at run time, and unloading and reloading code.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: What is the loader lock?
cards.a: A process-wide lock the loader holds while it loads and unloads modules and runs their entry points; DllMain and a DLL's global constructors and destructors run while it is held.

cards.q: Why can creating and waiting for a thread in DllMain deadlock?
cards.a: The new thread must run DLL_THREAD_ATTACH notifications, which need the loader lock, which the waiting DllMain holds.

cards.q: What is the alternative to doing work in DllMain?
cards.a: Explicit init and shutdown functions the program calls after loading and before unloading, or lazy initialisation on first use.

cards.q: Why can freeing memory across a DLL boundary crash?
cards.a: The two modules may use different copies of the C runtime with different heaps (static CRT, or Debug versus Release), so one module frees a block the other's heap never allocated.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: State the rule and three patterns that follow it.
cards.a: Whoever allocates, frees: the library offers a free function; the caller provides the buffer; or objects come with a create/destroy pair.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: Why not pass std::string across a DLL's C interface?
cards.a: Its layout and allocator can differ between the modules, so one side may misread or free the other's buffer.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: What does an exception barrier do?
cards.a: It wraps the body of an exported function in try/catch, catching specific exceptions, then std::exception, then everything, and returns an error code instead of letting anything escape.
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: Which three things must match for C++ types to cross a DLL boundary safely?
cards.a: The compiler and standard library version, the build configuration (iterator debug level), and the CRT setting so one heap is shared.
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: How do you pass a list of numbers through a C interface?
cards.a: As a pointer to the first element and a count, which the DLL can wrap in a span.
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: What is an opaque handle?
cards.a: A pointer to a type that is declared but not defined in the public header, so callers can pass it around but never depend on its contents.

cards.q: Why prefix every exported name?
cards.a: Exported names share one namespace in the process, so a prefix avoids collisions with other libraries and makes names predictable.

cards.q: Name three changes that are safe after publishing and three that are not.
cards.a: Safe: adding functions, adding result codes, changing what is behind a handle, adding enum values at the end. Unsafe: removing or renaming functions, changing parameters or return types, changing a visible struct's layout, renumbering enums.

cards.q: Give three rules for result codes in a stable interface.
cards.a: Explicit numbers that never change, new codes only at the end, and callers treating any unknown nonzero code as failure.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: How does a library report a detailed message through a C interface?
cards.a: It stores the message for the current thread when a call fails and offers a function that copies it into a caller-provided buffer.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: When is returning a const char* across the boundary safe?
cards.a: When it points to a string literal or other data that lives as long as the DLL and is never freed.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: What are the rules for growing a versioned struct?
cards.a: Add members only at the end; never remove, reorder or resize; give each new member a default for callers that did not send it.

cards.q: How does the library decide whether a member is present?
cards.a: It checks that the caller's size is at least the member's offset plus its size.

cards.q: Why are function tables popular for plugin and graphics APIs?
cards.a: One exported function gives the whole interface, and the table itself can be versioned and grown.

cards.q: What are the three methods of IUnknown and what does each do?
cards.a: QueryInterface asks for another interface the object supports; AddRef adds a reference; Release drops one and deletes the object at zero.

cards.q: How do COM-style interfaces evolve without breaking old callers?
cards.a: A published interface never changes. New methods go in a new interface that callers request with QueryInterface.

cards.q: Why does Release call delete this instead of the caller deleting the object?
cards.a: The memory is then freed by the module that allocated it, whoever releases the last reference.

cards.q: What does each part of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH mean for a DLL?
cards.a: Major: a breaking change. Minor: additions that keep compatibility. Patch: fixes with no interface change.

cards.q: State the compatibility rule for a program built against X.Y.Z.
cards.a: It works with any version that has the same major X and a minor.patch at least Y.Z.

cards.q: What was DLL Hell, and how does renaming the DLL for a new major version avoid it?
cards.a: Programs breaking because an installer replaced a shared DLL with an incompatible version of the same name. A new name lets both versions exist side by side.

cards.q: What does a header-only C++ wrapper add on top of a C interface?
cards.a: RAII ownership of handles, exceptions instead of result codes, and C++ types such as std::string, all compiled into the caller.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: What must the C destroy function accept for move-only wrappers to be simple?
cards.a: A null handle, doing nothing, so a moved-from wrapper can be destroyed safely.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: How does a reference-counting smart pointer behave on copy and on destruction?
cards.a: A copy calls AddRef; destruction calls Release.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: List the standard search order for a desktop application.
cards.a: Application folder, System32, the 16-bit System folder, the Windows folder, the current directory, then the PATH folders.

cards.q: Which two checks come before any folder is searched?
cards.a: Whether a module with that name is already loaded, and whether it is one of the known DLLs.

cards.q: Why is relying on PATH for your own DLLs a bad idea?
cards.a: PATH is searched last and differs between machines, so another DLL with the same name can be found first, or none at all.

cards.q: What three things together make a program load only the DLLs it means?
cards.a: Full paths built from a trusted folder for run-time loads, SetDefaultDllDirectories at start-up to restrict name-only loads, and checking files before loading them from writable folders.
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: How do you get the folder of your own .exe?
cards.a: GetModuleFileNameW with a null module handle, then take the parent folder.
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: How do you read a DLL's resources without running its code?
cards.a: Load it with LoadLibraryExW and LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE (with LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_IMAGE_RESOURCE).
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: What two linker settings turn on delay loading?
cards.a: /DELAYLOAD:name.dll for the DLL, and linking delayimp.lib.

cards.q: How does a program recover if a delay-loaded DLL is missing?
cards.a: Check availability first with __HrLoadAllImportsForDll, or provide a failure hook (__pfnDliFailureHook2) that returns a fallback.

cards.q: Name two things that cannot be delay-loaded.
cards.a: Exported data used directly, and kernel32.dll. (Calls made under the loader lock should not be delay-loaded either.)

cards.q: How is a four-part file version stored in VS_FIXEDFILEINFO?
cards.a: As two 32-bit values: major and minor in the high and low 16 bits of the MS value, build and revision in the LS value.

cards.q: Name the three ways to provide the Visual C++ runtime, and one drawback of each.
cards.a: The redistributable installer (needs an installer step), app-local copies (you must update them), the static runtime /MT (each module gets its own CRT and heap).

cards.q: Where should your own DLLs go when you ship?
cards.a: Next to the .exe, so the application folder, searched first, finds them; plugins in their own folders, loaded by full path.

cards.q: Name three things only a DLL can do.
cards.a: Be updated without rebuilding programs, be loaded and unloaded while running, share code pages between processes, and be called from other languages.

cards.q: When is a static library the right choice?
cards.a: When none of those are needed: it is the simplest option, with no extra files, no ABI design and no loading rules.

cards.q: How can one library be built either as a DLL or statically?
cards.a: With an export macro that expands to nothing when a STATIC symbol is defined, dllexport when building the DLL, and dllimport otherwise.

cards.q: What goes in a plugin contract header?
cards.a: The contract's version, the host's function table, the plugin's function table, and the name and type of the one exported function.

cards.q: List the checks a host makes before keeping a plugin.
cards.a: It is a .dll loaded by full path with safe search flags, it has the export, the returned table is big enough and has the right API version, and its start function succeeds.

cards.q: Why should a plugin do nothing in DllMain?
cards.a: DllMain runs under the loader lock; real work belongs in start, called after loading completes.

cards.q: What does the host do with a plugin's registrations when the plugin unloads?
cards.a: Removes every registration with that plugin as owner, before calling FreeLibrary.

cards.q: Why should the registry copy the id string?
cards.a: The plugin's string lives in the DLL's memory and disappears when it unloads; a copy also lets the registry use it as a map key safely.

cards.q: What are capabilities in a plugin contract?
cards.a: Named features with their own versions, so a plugin can require exactly what it uses and the contract can grow feature by feature.

cards.q: Describe the hot-reload loop.
cards.a: Watch the DLL's write time; when it changes and the file is complete, copy it to a fresh name, load the copy, get its function table, swap to the new table, then unload the old copy.

cards.q: Why does the PDB need a unique name per build?
cards.a: The debugger locks the PDB of the loaded DLL, so the linker could not overwrite it.

cards.q: Name three things that become invalid after unloading the old DLL.
cards.a: Its function pointers, its string literals, vtables of objects it created, and its static variables.

cards.q: Describe the host-owned-memory strategy.
cards.a: The host allocates one memory block and passes it to the DLL every frame; the DLL keeps all state as plain data in it, so swapping the DLL leaves the state untouched.

cards.q: What makes state safe to keep across a reload?
cards.a: Plain data with no vptrs, no pointers to the DLL's functions or string literals, and memory that came from the host rather than the DLL's heap.

cards.q: How do you handle a change in the state's layout?
cards.a: Store a version number, migrate older versions with defaults for new fields, and start fresh for versions you cannot read.

cards.q: Which course lessons does hot reload depend on?
cards.a: Run-time loading (2.03), versioned tables (3.03), the reload loop (5.03) and host-owned, versioned state (5.04).

cards.q: What makes plugin shutdown safe?
cards.a: Calling each plugin's stop in reverse load order, removing its registrations, dropping its pointers, and only then calling FreeLibrary.
